title: Eagle County, CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Eagle County wells have a median depth of 124 ft and a median yield of 15 gpm. Learn what that means for drilling and buying property here.
h1: Understanding water wells in Eagle County, Colorado
intro_html:
In Eagle County you’re almost always drilling into fractured mountain bedrock, not a big sand aquifer. That makes wells pretty site-specific, but the county has enough history to give you a realistic picture of depth, yield, and cost. These numbers come from thousands of permits spread around places like Vail, Eagle, Gypsum, Avon, Edwards, and the high-country areas.

If you’re buying land or planning a home on a well here, pay close attention to how deep nearby wells run and how much water they report. That’s what will drive both the drilling bill and how reliable your supply is over the long term.

sections.heading: How deep are wells in Eagle County, really
sections.html:
Across Eagle County, reported wells have a median total depth of 124 ft. The middle half fall between 58 and 260 ft, so that’s the range most drill bids will be based around for typical sites from Gypsum and Eagle up toward Avon and Vail.

Depths spread out quite a bit: 43% of wells are under 100 ft, another 37% land between 100 and 300 ft, and 18% run 300 to 600 ft. Only 2% go past 600 ft, but the deepest well on record reaches 3,800 ft, which shows how unpredictable fractured bedrock can be in spots.

For a new build, I’d plan financially for something in that 58–260 ft “middle half,” while knowing you could still hit a much deeper hole if your specific fracture system is tight.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the table
sections.html:
Static water levels in Eagle County are reasonably shallow for mountain country. The median depth to water is 40 ft, with the middle half of measurements between 20 and 114 ft below ground. That’s helpful for pump sizing and long-term power costs.

Looking over time, median measured water levels were around 26–32 ft in the 1970s–1980s, then dropped deeper into the 60–66 ft range in the 1990s–2000s. In the 2010s and 2020s, the median came back shallower, at 50 ft and then 38 ft.

That pattern doesn’t look like a steady decline; more like a system that responds to development and wet/dry cycles. Still, with only 304 wells reporting static levels, I’d treat it as a neighborhood-by-neighborhood question, especially in tighter canyons and higher benches.

sections.heading: Typical well yield and how much water to expect
sections.html:
On production, Eagle County wells look strong overall. The median reported yield is 15.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells are between 12.0 and 15.0 gpm. That’s plenty for a single home and even many small irrigated uses under a typical exempt household permit.

The distribution is encouraging: 69% of wells report 15+ gpm and 26% fall between 5 and 15 gpm. Only 4% are in the 1–5 gpm bracket, and just 1% report under 1 gpm.

In fractured rock, that still doesn’t guarantee your specific hole will be a high producer, but the odds of a totally marginal domestic well are fairly low compared with many other mountain counties. When you evaluate a parcel, look at actual gpm values from nearby wells, not just “adequate for domestic use” language.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and when
sections.html:
Eagle County has a long well history, with 4,665 wells in the state records. Drilling really ramped up in the 1980s and 1990s as mountain development took off. Permits jump from 276 in the 1970s to 556 in the 1980s, then peak at 1,448 in the 1990s.

Activity stayed strong with 766 permits in the 2000s and 478 in the 2010s, and there are already 305 permits in the 2020s, with records running through 2026. That means most properties around places like Edwards, Avon, and Wolcott have at least a few nearby wells you can look up.

A handful of drillers dominate the logs: Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne) shows 772 wells, Shelton Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Wayne) has 739, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 311 wells. Those records give you a solid dataset on depths and yields by area.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
In this county you’re drilling into fractured granite and gneiss, so contractors usually price per foot. The typical rate runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the 124 ft median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $8,100–$12,400.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical work, a finished domestic well at that median depth usually falls roughly in the $14,100–$24,400 range.

If you’re building on higher benches or ridges above places like Minturn, Red Cliff, or McCoy, I’d budget assuming you could land toward the deeper half of that 58–260 ft middle range, and make sure your financing can handle a deeper-than-expected bore.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
Even with a strong countywide median yield, there are still wells under 1 gpm and a few hundred in the low single digits. In fractured bedrock those low producers can sit right next to good wells. Always pull nearby well permits and look at both depth and gpm before closing.

There are also mapped environmental concerns: within about 10 miles, records show 25 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 44 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those don’t automatically mean your well is unsafe, but they’re a clear signal to review water testing history and plan your own lab work.

On small lots, pay attention to the distance between your proposed well, the septic system, and any irrigation or stock wells. Most permits here are domestic/household, but the county also has stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells that can complicate spacing.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Eagle County
sections.html:
Before you buy land in Eagle County, I’d start with the state well viewer and pull every permit within a reasonable radius. Note the total depth, yield, and static level for each, especially around places like Basalt, Dotsero, and Gypsum where geology can change over short distances.

Check the use type too: about 56% of wells are domestic/household, with the rest split among stock, irrigation, and a big chunk of monitoring wells. That mix tells you both about water demand and about where development has already probed the rock.

For a new home, confirm you can get the right kind of permit for your parcel, and talk with your driller about realistic depth and yield expectations based on nearby wells, not just the countywide medians.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Eagle County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported wells in Eagle County have a median depth of 124 ft, with the middle half between 58 and 260 ft. About 43% of wells are under 100 ft, another 37% run 100–300 ft, and 18% are 300–600 ft. Only 2% go deeper than 600 ft, but the single deepest well on record reaches 3,800 ft, showing how variable fractured bedrock can be.

faq.q: How much water do Eagle County wells usually produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield in Eagle County is 15.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells are between 12.0 and 15.0 gpm. Roughly 69% of wells report 15+ gpm and 26% come in between 5 and 15 gpm. Only 4% are in the 1–5 gpm range and 1% report under 1 gpm, so most domestic wells have solid production by Colorado mountain standards.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Eagle County?
faq.a: Static water level data here are limited, but the trend isn’t a simple decline. Median depth to water was 26–32 ft in the 1970s–1980s, then deepened to about 65–66 ft in the 1990s–2000s. In the 2010s and 2020s, medians improved to 50 ft and then 38 ft. With only 304 wells reporting static levels, you still need to look at local data for your specific area.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Eagle County, CO?
faq.a: In Eagle County’s fractured granite and gneiss, typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the 124 ft median depth, that puts the borehole itself around $8,100–$12,400. When you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished domestic well at that depth often totals roughly $14,100–$24,400, depending on site conditions and layout.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Eagle County?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location and needs to be tested, but there are some flags to be aware of. Within about 10 miles, records show 25 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 44 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those don’t automatically mean your well is contaminated, but they make professional lab testing for metals, PFAS, and basic potability especially important before relying on a well.
